appraisal_events.evidence: The duke retails Bloch's rout at Mme de Villeparisis's — his "sublimes" "donnés en veux-tu en voilà", Châtellerault kicking his shins unnoticed, the aunt's riposte "Hé, monsieur, que garderez-vous alors pour M. de Bossuet", and "M. Bloch n'a pas demandé son reste, il court encore"; the narrator adds the presentation to Mme Alphonse de Rothschild and Bloch's "Si j'avais su !", "exclamation dont la stupidité l'avait empêché de dormir pendant huit jours".
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch is made the table's comic material twice over: silenced by a wittier hostess and caught blurting out his own snobbery before a great name.

appraisal_events.evidence: Parenthetically: he pronounces Bloch's name in the German way "peut-être pour donner à un nom israélite l'air plus étranger"; he reddens at his own mention of Châtellerault's knee against a young woman; and he believes that "devant un nom célèbre, monsieur et une particule étaient essentiellement ancien régime" — that is, that "M. de Bossuet" is elegant usage.
appraisal_events.explanation: The same sentences that carry the duke's mockery expose him: petty ethnic malice, an embarrassed slip, and an ignorance of usage he takes for aristocratic refinement.

appraisal_events.evidence: She copies her husband's Germanic pronunciation "à court d'originalité à ce moment-là"; and when told there were no famous faces at the soirée she exclaims "comment ! il n'y avait pas de grands écrivains ! Vous m'étonnez, il y avait pourtant des têtes impossibles !" — "avouant par là que son respect pour les gens de lettres et son dédain du monde étaient plus superficiels qu'elle ne disait et peut-être même qu'elle ne croyait".
appraisal_events.explanation: Her professed reverence for writers is shown to be a pose she has half taken in herself, and her criterion for genius turns out to be an ugly face.

appraisal_events.evidence: "« Je crois que Mme de Villeparisis n'est pas absolument… morale », dit la princesse de Parme, qui savait qu'on n'allait pas chez la tante de la duchesse et, par ce que celle-ci venait de dire, voyait qu'on pouvait en parler librement"; seeing Mme de Guermantes look unapproving she retreats: "Mais à ce degré-là, l'intelligence fait tout passer."
appraisal_events.explanation: The aunt's disrepute is put into words at the table — society does not go to her house — but the narrator shows the judgment being licensed and then withdrawn according to what the duchesse seems to permit rather than by conviction.

status_effects.explanation: The passage's verdict on him is unmixed ridicule: his enthusiasm is tiresome, his riposte nonexistent, his one sincere word a piece of exposed snobbery.
His humiliation is not private: he was routed before Mme de Villeparisis's room and is now being replayed for the amusement of a ducal dinner table, his very name deformed in the telling.
Inside the retold scene she wins the exchange outright — "qui n'a pas sa langue dans sa poche" — with a line that ends the conversation and is still being quoted with relish.
Her standing is spoken of as compromised: people do not go to her house, and a princess feels free to question her morals aloud at another Guermantes table.
He comes off worse than the guest he is mocking, betrayed by his own parenthetical ignorance and malice.
She is caught borrowing her husband's joke for want of invention and confessing that her literary respect is skin-deep.

ambiguities: The diminishment of Bloch is delivered by narrators the passage is simultaneously undercutting: the duke's derision is exposed in the very sentence that carries it, so E1's negative weight rests on the narrator's own corroborating memory of the Rothschild blunder rather than on the table's authority.
